name: Apollo Lunar Module
description: A two-stage spacecraft that carried astronauts from lunar orbit to the surface and back.
purpose: The descent stage landed the crew on the Moon; the ascent stage returned them to the orbiting Apollo spacecraft.
overview: The Lunar Module (LM) was built specifically to operate in the Moon's airless environment. Its separate descent and ascent stages supported landing and crew return to lunar orbit.
whySent: Apollo needed a vehicle that could take two astronauts from lunar orbit to the surface and rendezvous with the Command and Service Module afterward.
missionInfo: Apollo 11's Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility in 1969. Six Apollo missions landed crews on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.
imageAlt: Buzz Aldrin descending the Apollo 11 Lunar Module ladder

name: Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV)
description: A battery-powered electric vehicle that let astronauts travel farther from their landing sites.
purpose: Extend crew mobility so astronauts could reach more geological locations and carry samples and equipment.
overview: The foldable Lunar Roving Vehicle was carried to the surface on Apollo 15, 16, and 17. Astronauts drove it during lunar surface traverses.
whySent: The later Apollo missions planned longer surface stays and wider scientific traverses; the rover increased the distance crews could cover.
missionInfo: Apollo 15 was the first mission to use the LRV. The crews used it to reach geological sites and transport samples and tools.
imageAlt: Apollo 17 lunar rover visible at the Taurus-Littrow site

name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)
description: A robotic spacecraft mapping the Moon and measuring its environment from orbit.
purpose: Map the lunar surface, study its terrain and resources, and support planning for future exploration.
overview: LRO carries instruments that observe the Moon from orbit, including cameras and a laser altimeter. Its measurements build detailed maps and characterize lunar conditions.
whySent: NASA launched LRO in 2009 to collect data useful for understanding the Moon and planning safe, informed future exploration.
missionInfo: LRO has studied the Moon from close orbit since 2009 and has imaged Apollo landing sites and other surface features.
imageAlt: LRO image showing the Apollo 12 landing site from lunar orbit

name: Curiosity Rover
description: A car-sized rover studying whether ancient Mars had environments that could support microbial life.
purpose: Analyze rocks, soil, and atmosphere to investigate Mars' past habitability and climate.
overview: Curiosity is a mobile laboratory equipped with cameras, a robotic arm, and instruments that study the chemistry and geology of Mars.
whySent: The Mars Science Laboratory mission was designed to assess whether Gale Crater ever offered environmental conditions favorable to microbial life.
missionInfo: Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in 2012 and continues its science exploration there.
imageAlt: Curiosity rover panorama beside Namib Dune in Gale Crater

name: Perseverance Rover
description: A rover exploring Jezero Crater and collecting rock and regolith samples for possible return to Earth.
purpose: Study ancient environments, search for signs of ancient microbial life, and collect and cache samples.
overview: Perseverance is a robotic geologist with cameras, spectrometers, and a sampling system. It explores the remains of an ancient lake and river delta in Jezero Crater.
whySent: Jezero preserves geological features that may record a watery past, making it a compelling place to investigate ancient habitability.
missionInfo: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on Feb. 18, 2021. Ingenuity traveled to Mars attached to the rover.
imageAlt: Perseverance rover view of the ancient Jezero Crater delta from its landing site

name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
description: A small solar-powered rotorcraft that demonstrated powered, controlled flight on another planet.
purpose: Test whether a rotorcraft could fly in Mars' thin atmosphere and demonstrate a new way to scout terrain.
overview: Ingenuity was a technology demonstration carried to Mars by Perseverance. Its flights tested autonomous flight in conditions very different from Earth.
whySent: The demonstration tested whether aerial vehicles could help future missions explore and select routes on Mars.
missionInfo: Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet in April 2021. NASA ended flight operations in January 2024 after rotor damage; the helicopter remains on Mars.
imageAlt: Ingenuity helicopter during its fourth flight on Mars, photographed by Perseverance

name: James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)
mission: NASA / ESA / CSA James Webb Space Telescope
description: A space observatory that studies the universe in infrared light, from nearby worlds to the earliest galaxies.
purpose: Observe faint and distant objects, study star and planet formation, and investigate exoplanet atmospheres.
overview: Webb uses a segmented primary mirror and infrared instruments to collect light from objects across the cosmos.
whySent: Infrared observations let astronomers study cooler objects and see through some cosmic dust that blocks visible light.
missionInfo: Webb launched in 2021 and operates near the Sun-Earth L2 point. It is an international partnership of NASA, ESA, and CSA.
imageAlt: Webb infrared image of the Cosmic Cliffs star-forming region

name: Hubble Space Telescope
description: A long-running space telescope observing the universe in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light.
purpose: Capture astronomical observations above Earth's atmosphere to study stars, galaxies, planets, and cosmic evolution.
overview: Hubble is a robotic observatory in low Earth orbit. Its instruments collect light across several wavelengths, and astronauts serviced it during Space Shuttle missions.
whySent: Putting a telescope above Earth's atmosphere gives it a clear view without atmospheric distortion and absorption.
missionInfo: Hubble launched in 1990 and continues to make scientific observations. NASA and ESA developed the mission together.
imageAlt: Astronauts servicing Hubble Space Telescope during a Shuttle mission

name: Voyager 1
description: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn before continuing outward into interstellar space.
purpose: Study the outer planets and their moons, then measure the environment beyond the Sun's heliosphere.
overview: Voyager 1 is a robotic flyby spacecraft carrying scientific instruments and a Golden Record with sounds and images from Earth.
whySent: The Voyager program took advantage of a rare outer-planet alignment to study Jupiter and Saturn and continue exploration beyond the planets.
missionInfo: Launched Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 encountered Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012.
imageAlt: NASA/JPL artist concept of a Voyager spacecraft with its high-gain antenna pointed toward Earth; the design represents Voyager 1 and its twin

name: Voyager 2
description: Voyager 2 explored Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, then continued its journey beyond the heliosphere.
purpose: Study the outer planets and their moons during flybys, then measure the space environment beyond the Sun's heliosphere.
overview: Voyager 2 is a robotic flyby spacecraft and the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune. It carries scientific instruments and a Golden Record with sounds and images from Earth.
whySent: A rare outer-planet alignment let Voyager 2 use gravity assists to continue from Jupiter and Saturn to Uranus and Neptune.
missionInfo: Launched Aug. 20, 1977, Voyager 2 encountered Jupiter and Saturn, then Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. It crossed into interstellar space in November 2018.
imageAlt: Neptune with the Great Dark Spot, imaged by Voyager 2 four days before closest approach
